1.
The Appellant has preferred this Appeal against the judgment and order dated 12.5.2022 passed by the Special Judge, Satara in Special POCSO Case No.53/2017.

The Appellant was convicted for commission of the offence punishable under Section 5(j)
(ii), 5(l) read with Section 6 of the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012 (for short,
'POCSO Act').

entities.text: Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012
entities.label: STATUTE

sentences.text: He was sentenced to suffer R.I. for ten years and to pay a fine of Rs.10,000/- in default to Deshmane(PS) 908-apeal-1259-23-J.odt suffer RI for six months.

He was not convicted for the offence punishable under Section 376(2)(n) of IPC and Section 3(a) read with Section 4 of the POCSO Act as, according to the learned Judge, the conviction under Section 6 of the POCSO Act is stringent and more effective in the nature.
He was granted set off under Section 428 of Cr.P.C. for the period which he had undergone in custody since 11.7.2017 till the judgment and order of convicting and sentencing him was passed.

Heard Ms. Trupti Khamkar, learned counsel for the Appellant, Ms. Ranjana Humane, learned APP for the Respondent No.1-State and Ms. Padmaja Malgaonkar, learned counsel for the Respondent No.2.
3.
The prosecution case, in brief, is that the victim in this case was 14 years of age.
She was studying in a school and was staying in hostel.
She had come back to her parents during the summer vacation in the year 2017.
During that period, the Appellant established physical relations with her against her wish.
When her school reopened, routine medical check-up was conducted and at that time it was revealed that she was pregnant.
The Headmaster of the school 908-apeal-1259-23-J.odt informed the victim's father who took her back to his house.
She was then taken to a private doctor.
Her pregnancy was confirmed.
The FIR was lodged vide C.R. No.92/2017 at Medha police station.
The victim was sent for medical examination.
Subsequently her pregnancy was medically terminated.
Her blood samples were collected.
The samples of the fetus were also collected.
The Appellant was arrested on 11.7.2017.
His blood sample for DNA testing was also collected.
All these samples were sent to the Forensic Science Laboratory for DNA analysis.
The samples were sent on 15.7.2017.
In the meantime, the investigation proceeded.
The statements of various witnesses were recorded.
The spot panchnama was conducted.
The DNA analysis showed that the Appellant and the victim were the biological parents of the product of conception.
After the investigation was concluded, the charge-sheet was filed and the case was tried before the learned Special Judge.
4. During the trial, the prosecution examined thirteen witnesses including the victim, her father, a pancha, the medical officers and the police officers.

Another important witness was an expert who had conducted the DNA test on the samples sent to the 908-apeal-1259-23-J.odt FSL.
5.

The defence of the Appellant was of denial, and, in addition he stated in the statement recorded under Section 313 of Cr.P.C. that there was a quarrel between the victim's parents on one side and the Appellant's in-laws on the other; resulting in lodging this false FIR against him.
6. The learned Judge considered the evidence on record and the defence taken by the Appellant.
After considering the arguments in that behalf, the learned Judge passed the order of conviction and sentenced him as mentioned earlier.
7. The main witness in this case is the victim herself.
The FIR was lodged by her father who was examined as PW-1.
He has deposed that he had three daughters.
The victim was studying in the 8 th standard in an ashram shala at a different place.
The victim had come to their house because of her summer vacation after her annual examinations were over.
After the summer vacation, PW-1 took her back to the ashram shala on 2.6.2017.
On 30.6.2017, the Headmaster Mr. Zalte (examined as PW-9) informed PW-1 telephonically that the 908-apeal-1259-23-J.odt medical examination had revealed that the victim was pregnant.
PW-1 took her back to their house.
On enquiries with her she named the Appellant as the person who had physical relations with her.
She told PW-1 that the Appellant had threatened to kill her if she disclosed that incident to anyone else.
The incident had taken place during the summer vacation in their own house.
The Appellant was the son-in- law of PW-1's cousin and was residing in PW-1's cousin's house.
PW-1 took the victim to the civil hospital.
Her pregnancy was confirmed.

sentences.text: Certain questions were asked to her to bring out some omissions from her police statement but those omissions were not directly related to the incident involving the Appellant making her pregnant.
The two contradictory portions marked A & B were shown to her and they were subsequently proved through the evidence of the Police Naik Latika Kawale.

One of the portions mentions that on 15.7.2017 their school started but she was taken to the school on 22.7.2017.
This portion at Exhibit-47 is not relevant because this is unrelated to the main events.
The second exhibited portion i.e. Exhibit-48 mentions that when she went back to the school her medical examination was conducted on 28.7.2017.
The defence 908-apeal-1259-23-J.odt wants to take advantage of these dates.
However, obviously those dates were wrongly written as '15.7.2017' and '28.7.2017' because her statement itself was recorded on '11.7.2017'.

Therefore, the defence cannot get any benefit from this mistake in the dates mentioned in her police statement; though they are proved through the evidence of the officer PW-5 who had written her statement.
At one point in her cross- examination she stated that Medha police had taken her for recording of her statement.

At that time her father was with her and the police had told her to say that the Appellant had established the physical relations with her though it is not elaborated in the cross-examination as to exactly when this statement was recorded; but it appears that it was in reference to her statement recorded under Section 164 of CrP.C..

22. I have considered these submissions.
As far as age of the victim is concerned, the prosecution has relied on the evidence of PW- 8 the Headmaster of the concerned school who has produced the school record.
According to her school record, her date of birth was 13.10.2003.
There is no reason to dispute this school record and there is no cross-examination effectively challenging the school record.
The date of incident is from somewhere in April and May, 2017.
Therefore, at that time she was less than fourteen years of age.
The fact that she was a minor at that time is further supported by the radiological examination of the victim conducted by PW-4 Ulka Zende.
According to her, the victim was seven weeks and six days pregnant on 10.7.2017.
This witness had produced the certificate of radiological examination at Exhibit-45A which showed the age of the victim between fourteen years to fifteen & half years.
Therefore, the prosecution has proved beyond any doubt that the victim was below eighteen years of age at the time of the incident which had taken place in April-May, 2017.
The next question would be who was responsible for committing the offence.
In this context, the evidence of the victim herself is clear enough and she has named the Appellant as the offender.

I do not find force in the submissions of learned counsel for the Appellant that the incident could not have taken place when the victim's parents had gone to some other village and when she was present in the house along with her three sisters and that it was not possible that the incident could have taken place without anybody else noticing it.

The defence cannot run away from the fact that the Ashok Shankar Mane vs State Of Maharashtra And Anr. on 6 August, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/101061318/

24. The next question would be the result of the DNA analysis.
Learned counsel for the Appellant submitted that there was a strong possibility of tampering with the samples.
She tried to contend that the samples of the victim and the product of conception were taken on 12.7.2017 and were sent on 15.7.2017.
However, the evidence, as discussed above, shows that the samples were in fact collected on 14.7.2015.
Pregnancy was terminated on 14.7.2015.
Therefore, 908-apeal-1259-23-J.odt sample of the product of conception was not taken on 12.7.2015.
The covering letter to the FSL was also on the same date and it was sent to the FSL, Pune and it was received at Pune on 15.7.2017.
Therefore, there was no discrepancy in the prosecution evidence and there is no scope to infer that there was a strong opportunity of tampering with the samples.
The DNA report shows that the victim and the Appellant were the biological parents of the product of conception.

It would be too far-fetched to accept that the police knew the real culprit and that he was other than the present Appellant and that they sent a sample of that real culprit to the FSL instead of the samples of the Appellant.

Only then the argument of tampering with the evidence can be taken to the logical end because the DNA clearly shows that the samples received by the FSL showed the samples were of the biological parents of the product of conception.
25. PW-11 Rohidas Mundhe has stated that the samples were received intact in sealed condition.
Considering these submissions, I do not find force in the submissions of learned counsel for the Appellant that possibility of tampering with the samples cannot be ruled out.

In this background,
the DNA report can be seen which is 908-apeal-1259-23-J.odt produced on record at Exhibit-109.
26.

The DNA report consists of STR locus values.
27. PW-11 was extensively cross-examined regarding the procedure for conducting the analysis.
The data maintained under the chart and the method of STR locus was part of the Report.
The defence was accorded full opportunity to cross-examine the witness on all these aspects.
PW-11 Rohidas Mundhe had withstood this extensive cross-examination.
Therefore, there is no reason to disbelieve the evidence of the prosecution in respect of this DNA analysis.

2. The Investigating Officer shall be responsible for the transportation of the DNA evidence to the concerned police station or the hospital concerned, as the case may be.
He shall also be responsible for ensuring that the samples so taken reach the concerned forensic science laboratory with dispatch and in any case not later than 48- hours from the time of collection.
Should any extraneous circumstance present itself and the 48-hours timeline cannot be complied with, the reason for the delay shall be duly recorded in the case diary.
Throughout, the requisite efforts be made to preserve the samples as per the requirement corresponding to the nature of the sample taken.

3. In the time that the DNA samples are stored pending trial appeal etc., no package shall be opened,
altered or resealed without express authorisation of the Trial Court acting upon a statement of a duly qualified and experienced medical professional to the effect that the same shall not have a negative impact on the sanctity of the evidence and with the Court being 908-apeal-1259-23-J.odt assured that such a step is necessary for proper and just outcome of the Investigation/Trial.

4. Right from the point of collection to the logical end, i.e., conviction or acquittal of the Accused, a Chain of Custody Register shall be maintained wherein each and every movement of the evidence shall be recorded with counter sign at each end thereof stating also the reason therefor.
This Chain of Custody Register shall necessarily be appended as part of the Trial Court record.
Failure to maintain the same shall render the I.O. responsible for explaining such lapse.

The Directors General of Police of all the States shall prepare sample forms of the Chain of Custody Register and all other documentation directed above and ensure its dispatch to all districts with necessary instruction as may be required."
